newsitem.title: FRANCE: UNESCO accord on genetic research ethics delayed.
newsitem.headline: UNESCO accord on genetic research ethics delayed.

text.p: A UNESCO expert committee has put off for at least two months its final approval of a draft declaration of ethical guidelines for genetic research, UNESCO officials said on Monday.

UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee (IBC), which had been expected to approve its draft "Universal Declaration on the Human Genome and Human Rights" on Friday, instead sent the document back to a subcommittee for fine-tuning, UNESCO official Georges Kutukjian said.
"It has been approved by the committee in its broad outlines, conditional on certain proposals which will be taken up at a special meeting on December 16-17," Kutukjian told Reuters.

The draft guidelines state that human genetics research holds vast potential but must be regulated to protect public health and "to guard against any eugenic practice that runs counter to human dignity and human rights".

It states that the genetic material found in every human cell is "the common heritage of humanity" and cautions that peoples' genetic makeup should never be used as a basis for granting or denying their rights.

Kutukjian said committee members mainly sought modifications in the declaration's structure and phrasing rather than in its substance, suggesting some organisational changes and a strengthening of the language in some sections.

If all differences are resolved at the mid-December meeting, the declaration would next be referred to UNESCO member states and additional experts, with an eye to its adoption as an international convention next year.
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) created the IBC in 1993 to monitor developing ethical issues in genetic research and engineeering.
The panel's 55 experts hail from 40 countries and include doctors and scientists as well as philosophers and lawyers.
